MEETING TYPE: Regular Council Meeting
To:
Council
From:
Jackie Trenholm, Deputy Clerk
 Date:
April 16, 2025
 Subject:
2026 Municipal Election Matters
 Report No.:
2025-529
TITLE: 2026 Municipal Election Matters
RECOMMENDATION:
THAT Council authorizes the passing of By-law No. 25-25, Being a By-law Relating to 2026
Municipal Election Matters (language(s) to be used for election forms/notices/information; use
of alternative voting method; use of vote-counting equipment).
PURPOSE:
The purpose of this recommendation is to enable Council to make certain decisions respecting
the 2026 Municipal Election, including the use of the "telephone/internet" voting method.
BACKGROUND:
Several items must be addressed relative to the 2026 Municipal Election, including:
1.    Use of Alternative Voting Methods
2.    Advance Poll
3.    Early Voting and/or Reduced Voting Hours
4.    Use of vote-counting equipment
5.    Language(s) in Notices/Forms/Information
6.    Payment of rebate for campaign contributions
7.    Ward(s) review/changes
8.    Electronic filing of financial statements
9.    Submitting a By-law or question to the electors (question on the ballot)
10.  Appointment of Compliance Committee
DISCUSSION:
Item No. 1: Use of Alternative Voting Methods

The Municipality had been employing the vote-by-mail (VBM) voting method for several prior
general municipal elections (2003, 2006, 2010 and 2014). This alternative voting method has
been successful, having yielded higher voter turnout rates over traditional elections in each of
the last four general elections.
While this method has increased voter turnout, compared to the traditional in-person polls, the
participation rate has decreased over the last decade-and-a-half, as follows:
•    Voter turnout 2003 – 60.61%
•    Voter turnout 2006 – 57.72%
•    Voter turnout 2010 – 56.86%
•    Voter turnout 2014 – 55.95%
Given this gradual, but steady, decline in voter participation, staff recommended the use of the
telephone/internet voting method in the 2018 general election, the 2020 by-election and the
2022 general election. Voter turnout for those elections was as follows:
•    2018 General Election –     55.21% 
•    2020 By-election –    32.48%
•    2022 General Election -  33.10%
Given the trend in municipal elections, across Ontario, of having fewer voters participate in
such elections, achieving a 55.21% voter turnout in 2018 was excellent, and placed Sioux
Lookout in among the highest of voter turnout results in Ontario. By-elections typically result in
lower number of voters. The 2020 By-election turnout was approximately 2.5% higher than the
last by-election in 2015. The 2022 voter turnout was lower than the 2018 general election.
When there isn’t a mayoral race, voter turnout is typically lower.
Vote-by-Mail versus Telephone/Internet Voting – An Analysis
Election Principles
Despite which voting method is selected, it is the responsibility of the Clerk/Returning Officer
to uphold the following election principles:
•    The secrecy and confidentiality of the individual votes is paramount;
•    The election must be fair and non-biased;
•    The election must be accessible to all voters;
•    The integrity of the process must be maintained throughout the election;
•    There must be certainty that the results of the election reflect the votes cast; and
•    All voters and candidates must be treated fairly and consistently. 
Vote by Mail – Overview
Electors receive a voting kit in the mail. They mail in their signed declaration form along with
their secrecy envelope containing their marked ballot. The declaration form is scanned prior to
voting day; the secrecy ballot is kept in a secure ballot box until the close of election. On
Election Day, Staff open the ballot boxes containing the secrecy envelopes and review each
ballot to determine if the ballot is spoiled or rejected. Staff then feed the ballots through a vote
tabulating machine or count them manually. Once all of the ballots have been fed through the
vote tabulator (or counted manually), the tabulator totals the votes and provides a printable
receipt of the results to election officials, or the totals of votes cast and counted manually are

reported to the Returning Officer.
Advantages and Disadvantages: Vote-by-mail (VBM)
Advantages:
Signed  declaration  –  provides  security against voter fraud
Improved size and efficiency. Desk top tabulators are hooked up to a PC laptop and can
scan 40 ballots per minute and results are quick. They also store the image of each
ballot for recount/audit purposes.
Longer voting period
Disadvantages:
With VBM, staff are required to facilitate vote tabulation by feeding ballots into vote
tabulators, or physically/manually examining each ballot, and must make a determination
with respect to spoiled and rejected ballots
Staff resources and time - secrecy ballot envelopes cannot be opened until close of
voting. Ballots must then be organized, reviewed, scanned, counted and then eventually
destroyed.
If not using vote-counting equipment, manual vote-counting is extremely time consuming
– unofficial results in 2014 were not available until 2:00 a.m. (6 hours after close of
voting).
Opportunity for Spoiled ballots – vote does not count (e.g. elector included ballot with
signed declaration card; no signed declaration form or no declaration form included;
marking on the ballot that does not indicate choice or there is no marking on ballot)
Spoiled ballots – the voter has no way of knowing if their ballot was spoiled. There is no
confirmation process.
Potential to receive voter kits by unintended recipient which includes the ballot
Postal service – takes five days for voter to receive vote by mail kit; takes five days for
municipal office to receive marked ballot with secrecy envelope (total 5-10 days) by mail,
unless dropped off at municipal office
Costs – more expensive voting method due to need for more staff; manual count;
training of staff, etc.
Internet/Telephone Voting - Overview
Internet Voting – Electors receive a Voter Information Letter containing a Personal
Identification Number (PIN) in the mail. They log onto the election server on any computer,
vote by using their keyboard in response to a virtual ballot, the vote is stored on the election
software. The elector receives confirmation of their vote by way of a confirmation number or
printable receipt. At the close of Election Day, the internet software totals the votes received
and provides a printable receipt of the results to election officials.
Telephone Voting – Electors receive a Voter Information Letter containing a Personal
Identification Number (PIN) in the mail. They call a toll-free number from a touchtone phone;
vote by pressing buttons in response to a voice recording and the vote is stored by the
election software. The elector receives confirmation of their vote by way of a confirmation
number. At the close of Election Day, the telephone voting results are combined with the
internet voting results for one total result. A printable receipt of the results is made available to
election officials.

It is recommended that both internet and telephone options be provided to electors for the
2026 municipal election.
Advantages and Disadvantages of Internet/Telephone Voting
Advantages:
Less staff and administrative resources required and less expensive overall (except in
first year of implementation, due to public education costs)
No ballot errors/spoiled ballots because the software does not permit it. There are built in
reminders or safeguards to prevent accidental voting
Voter is provided with confirmation that their vote counted by issuance or confirmation of
a receipt
Elector participation is real time and results are immediate
Ballot destruction after election is electronically completed and verified
Voter has the opportunity to review selection and make changes prior to submitting vote
Lowered carbon footprint; environmentally sustainable due to less paper required
Recounts are instantaneous and inexpensive
Most accessible form of voting. Allows persons with disabilities the opportunity to
completely mark their ballot in private without the assistance of a designated friend or
election official, therefore providing greater dignity
Disadvantages:
Not everyone has access to a computer or is computer literate; however, telephone
voting would be the alternative to those who do not have internet access or low levels of
computer literacy
Security and viruses; voter authentication - however, the preferred vendor has
implemented robust measures to mitigate such threats
Telephone voting takes time – audio ballot
Telephone voting - Voter cannot see the names of the candidates
Other Benefits of Internet/telephone Voting
•    provides convenience, accommodates changing lifestyles, demanding work schedules;
•    enhances accessibility for students studying away from home, those travelling, shift
workers, infirmed persons, and persons with language barriers.
•    for persons with disabilities, it provides greater dignity and privacy for electors;
•    engages a wider range of age demographics, provides greater accuracy and fast results, is
convenient for seasonal residents, and has the potential for increased voter turnout.
Public Education & Outreach
Public education and outreach will play a critical role in the 2026 municipal election, should the
telephone/internet voting method be adopted. Although this method has been used several
times in Sioux Lookout, to ensure that concerns and questions regarding this voting method
are adequately addressed, a prior election education campaigns will be enhanced and
administered by the Clerk.
In order to mitigate concerns regarding accessibility for senior citizens to vote, the Clerk, as in
the 2018, 2020 and 2022 elections, will arrange to attend multi-residential senior complexes
throughout the community to provide senior citizens the opportunity to vote at their residence.
Additionally, for those who are not comfortable with internet voting or telephone voting on their
own, an electronic voting station will be established at the Municipal Office, with staff on hand

to provide assistance, as requested. Furthermore, remote voting locations will be established
at the Sioux Lookout Senior’s Centre, the Sioux Lookout Meno Ya Win Health Centre, the
William George Extended Care Unit, the Nishnawbe-Gamik Friendship Centre, and in Hudson.
Accessibility for Persons with Disabilities
Internet/Telephone voting offers the most accessible form of voting.  Voters are offered the
greatest secrecy and less assisted voting thereby enhancing the quality of the vote and
anonymity.
Security
Section 89 of the Municipal Elections Act provides for penalties for any contravention of the
Act, as follows:
A person is guilty of an offence if he or she,
(a)    votes without being entitled to do so;
(b)    votes more times than this Act allows;
(c)    votes in a voting place in which he or she is not entitled to vote;
(d)    induces or procures a person to vote when that person is not entitled to do so;
(e)    having appointed a voting proxy that remains in force, votes otherwise than by the proxy;
(f)    having been appointed a voting proxy, votes under the authority of the proxy when the
elector has cancelled the proxy, is no longer entitled to vote or has died;
(g)   before or during an election, publishes a false statement of a candidate’s withdrawal;
(h)   furnishes false or misleading information to a person whom this Act authorizes to obtain
information;
(i)    without authority, supplies a ballot to anyone;
(j)    delivers to the deputy returning officer to be placed in a ballot box a paper other than the
ballot the deputy returning officer gave him or her;
(k)    takes a ballot away from the voting place;
(l)    at an election, takes, opens or otherwise deals with a ballot, a ballot box, or a book or
package of ballots without having authority to do so;
(m)  attempts to do something described in clauses (a) to (l)
Clearly, accountability of voting rests with the voter and there are penalties associated with
voter fraud. Unsupervised voting facilitates the potentiality of these offences. Voter
impersonation, coercion and fraud are concerns which are mitigated through the design of any
voting system, regardless of whether it is a supervised or unsupervised model.
Item No. 2: Advance Poll
The use of the vote-by-mail or telephone/internet voting methods eliminates the need for
advance polls. Additionally, determination of this matter has now been delegated to the Clerk,
via the Municipal Elections Act, Council no longer makes these decisions.
Item No. 3: Early Voting and/or Reduced Voting Hours
The vote-by-mail voting or telephone/internet voting methods eliminates the need for these
measures. Additionally, determination of this matter has now been delegated to the Clerk, via
the Municipal Elections Act, Council no longer makes these decisions.
Item No. 4: Use of Vote-Counting Equipment

The Municipality had used Electronic Vote Tabulators (EVTs) in the 2000, 2003, 2006 and
2010 Municipal Elections. Ballots were created and coded by Ward, School Board
candidate(s) and Municipal Council (Mayor and Councillors-at-Large) candidates and
processed by the EVT on voting day. In the past, this has resulted in election results within
minutes of the close of polls.
For the 2014 Municipal Election, the Clerk chose to use manual vote-counting procedures
given that vote-counting equipment rental had significantly increased in cost increase since
the 2010 Municipal Election. The primary impact on the election was a longer time-frame
between the close of polls and the announcement of the unofficial results – a total of six hours.
If Council chooses to use the Vote-by-Mail voting method in 2026, vote tabulators will be
required to ensure the efficient tabulation of results; this is an additional cost to using this
voting method.
Item No. 5: Language(s) in Notices/Forms/Information
Prescribed forms (those set by legislation) must be provided in English only, but may be
provided in English and French only. Other forms/notices/information can be provided in
English, French or any other language, providing Council passes a by-law permitting such.
In one previous election, prior to 2003, some of the Notices were provided in both English and
Oji-Cree. This exercise was costly and was subsequently discontinued. It should be noted that
the onus is on the elector to provide translation services when voting. In 2003, 2006 and 2010,
the Clerk recommended and Council passed a By-law to provide notices in Oji-Cree at the
discretion of the Clerk.
Staff recommends that Council permit notices to be published in Oji-Cree for the 2026
Municipal Election, at the discretion of the Clerk.
Item No. 6: Payment of Rebate for Campaign Contributions
Council may pass a by-law for the payment of rebates to persons who make contributions to
candidates running for Council. The payment of these funds come from general Municipal
funds (i.e., from the Sioux Lookout taxpayer). There is significant work involved in setting-up
and administering this process. Seasoned Municipal practitioners recommend against this
practice.
Staff recommends that Council not implement a system for rebates for campaign
contributions.
Item No.7: Ward(s) Review/Changes
On September 19, 2012, Council passed By-law No. 50-12, Being a By-law to Restructure the
Ward System in the Municipality of Sioux Lookout. This By-law eliminated Ward 2 (Sioux
Lookout). The effect of this change was that in the 2014 Municipal Election, the number of
"Councillors-at-Large" to be elected increased from four to five, in addition to the Ward 1
(Hudson) Councillor and the Mayor.
Council had expressed interest in reviewing the remaining Ward (Ward 1, Hudson) to
determine the value in retaining it as Sioux Lookout’s only Ward. The Clerk presented Council

with the results of the 2021 Ward Boundary Review and recommended the elimination of the
sole remaining Ward (Ward 1 (Hudson). Council passed By-law No. 103-21 Being a By-law to
Dissolve Ward 1 (Hudson), the only remaining ward within the Municipality of Sioux Lookout,
effective for the 2022 general Municipal Election.
As such, there is no longer a requirement for a Ward Boundary Review.
Item No. 8: Electronic Filing of Financial Statements
Prior to recent changes to the Municipal Elections Act, Sec. 78 (7) empowered the council of a
local municipality to pass a by-law to authorize the filing of financial statements in an electronic
format. This matter has now been delegated to the Clerk.
To facilitate the timely submission of Financial Statements, and in recognition of the trends
towards the increasing use of electronic measures/systems, the Clerk intends to provide for
this type of filing. Traditional "hard copy" filing of Financial Statements may be accepted.
Item No. 9: Submitting a By-law or Question to the Electors
This matter will be dealt with in a separate Report, closer to the deadline for making such a
decision (i.e., March 1, 2026). 
Item No. 10: Appointment of Compliance Audit Committee
The appointment of a Compliance Audit Committee is a requirement under the Municipal
Elections Act (Sec. 88.37 (1)). This matter will be dealt with in a separate report to be brought
before Council prior to October 1, 2026.
RELATIONSHIP TO THE STRATEGIC PLAN:
This is a routine administrative matter with no direct link to Council’s Strategic Plan.
FINANCIAL IMPLICATIONS:
The estimated cost for Vote-by-Mail for the 2026 municipal election is $52,890.
The estimated cost for telephone/internet voting for the 2026 municipal election is $26,700.
Staff highly recommends not using both the telephone/internet and vote-by-mail options.
Investigation into this matter revealed that this dual-method option is undesirable for the
following reasons:
•    Significantly higher costs
•    Confusion for electors
•    Greater challenges in administering the election
•    Greater chance for voter fraud
Council, as per previous elections, has been setting aside money in the Elections Reserve

since 2019 to ensure there are sufficient funds available for the 2026 election, and to save
having to budget for the entire election amount in 2026.

events.

performances scheduled for the 8th, 15th, 22nd, and 29th. This concert series aims to 
showcase the new venue and generate interest in future rentals.

series in advance of the first concert date on August 8th. For future Town-run events, staff 
will seek sponsorship to support these initiatives.

Background: Status updates on approved capital projects serve as a monitoring 
mechanism for staff and provide information to Council. This represents best practice in 
open and accountable municipal operations. 
Council will be able to track the status of projects that have been approved for completion 
with taxpayer's money and grant money received by the municipality. 
A Capital Status Update was distributed to Directors and operational Managers on July 22nd , 
2024. They were asked to provide a status update and project comments to share with 
Council. This is an opportunity to identify any project challenges and whether the project 
can still be completed on schedule and on budget. 
On November 21St, 2023, Council passed By-Law 78-2023 to adopt the 2024 Operating 
and Capital Budget.

invoices for 2023, the budget carry-forward for these 51 projects was $5,432,045.

Subject: Wiarton District Optimist Club Community Grant Program Final Report -
Canada Day Event Support 
Recommendation: That Council receives the final report from the Wiarton District Optimist 
Club as it relates to the Community Grant Program allocation to support the Wiarton Canada 
Day event. 
Link to Strategic Planning: Goal 1: Transparent and Accountable Governance, Goal 
3: Collaboration and Partnerships and Goal 4: Healthy, Vibrant and Safe Communities 
would be the general links to the Strategic Plan. 
Specific Objectives and Actions would be: 
3.1 
Maximize Shared Services and Resources 
3.1.1 Explore formal and informal opportunities to collaborate for expanded service 
delivery, reduced cost and improved community benefit 
Background: The Community Grant Program Policy (TR.18.2) was adopted by Council 
in 2021 as a means to streamline the requests that Council receives from members of 
the community seeking funding . The policy has undergone amendments since its initial 
adoption with the last amendment being adopted in 2024. One of the requirements in 
the policy is that the grant recipients are required to make a final report 90 days 
following their event or by November 30, 2024, whichever is earlier. 
The 2024 program application period closed on November 30, 2023 with eighteen (18) 
submissions being received. Two of the applicants did not receive funding as they did not 
meet the program criteria, proposing projects for Town and other Government Agency 
property. Subsequent to deliberations, Council adopted resolution R-07-2024 wherein 
funding awards were decided and additionally, Council decided to remove the previous 
"automatically recurring" grants which staff had been including in the annual budgets. Using 
the last remaining budget allocation, Council has also provided funding support to two 
additional organizations since the original allocation of funding. 

Staff have received the final report from the Wiarton District Optimist Club which supported 
the annual Canada Day event held in Bluewater Park. The grant allocation was $500. 
The final report from the Wiarton District Optimist Club explains that the event had vendors, 
a BBQ, a pancake breakfast and family entertainment. The Wiarton District Optimist Club 
was fortunate in that they secured several local sponsors and funding through the Celebrate 
Canada Grant Program. All of the funds, including those from the Town allowed them to 
hold a family friendly event which they feel was a success. The Optimist Club was able to 
finish the event with a surplus of $2,839.08. The Town's donation was directed toward the 
Bluewater Park rental costs. 
Options: 
a) 
Receive the final report, as presented. 
b) 
Seek additional information from the Wiarton District Optimist Club. 
Attachments:

Community Grant Program Policy (TR.18.2) 
Two 
Grant Award Letter and Resolution R-07-2024

budget. The Community Grant Program is included as part of the Council budget. The 
Parks, Recreation and Culture Department have many detailed discussions with community 
groups and provides encouragement to those groups to apply for funding . The Legislative 
Services Department collects applications and, together with the Parks, Recreation and 
Culture Department, analyzes them against the policy criteria. The Legislative Services 
Department makes recommendations to Council and provides to Council, the final reports 
from the grant recipients. The Financial Services Department processes the award 
payments.

Community Grant Program.

Bluewater Park facility rental. They have demonstrated that the Town funds have been 
expended.

additional information from the organization. If that is the case, staff will bring an additional 
report to a future meeting.

Community Grant Program 
1.0 
Purpose 
The Town of South Bruce Peninsula has established the Community Grant Program to: 
• 
Improve the well-being of individuals, neighbourhoods and the municipality as 
a whole by directing Community Grant funding to eligible recipients who can 
demonstrate the greatest need in the community while supporting Council's 
strategic priorities. 
• 
Diversify the availability of activities available to all residents of our 
community and contribute to enhancing the quality of life. 
• 
Through this support, it is hoped that other funding may be leveraged, and 
participants and volunteers can be supported, attracted and retained. 
• 
Ensure that the process to review and allocate Community Grant funding is 
transparent, consistent and achieves the optimal impact for the investment 
provided. 
2.0 
Authority 
This policy is established pursuant to Section 107 of the Municipal Act, 2001 which 
allows a municipality, subject to Section 106, to make grants, on such terms as to 
security and otherwise as the Council considers appropriate, to any person, group or 
body, including a fund , within or outside the boundaries of the municipality for any 
purpose that Council considers to be in the interests of the municipality. 
3.0 
Budget 
On an annual basis, Council will determine the total funding envelope for Community 
Grants as part of the annual operating budget. 
As the number of grant requests may exceed funds available and budget priorities may 
change from year to year, applicants are not guaranteed funding . A Community Grant 
approved in any year is not considered a commitment by the Town to continue financial 
assistance in future years.

4.0 
Activities Eligible for Funding 
The Community Grant Program will provide grants to support eligible community-based 
organizations for community-based activities. 
Applications must align with one or more of the Town's strategic priorities. 
An activity funded by a Community Grant must be open to the public at minimal or no 
charge and must be accessible to all community members by satisfying the 
requirements of the Ontario Human Rights Code, the Charter of Rights and Freedoms, 
and the Accessibility for Ontarians with Disabilities Act. 
The Community Grant Program is intended to provide funding that is supplemental to 
the overall financial requirements to carry on a planned activity. The Community Grant 
Program is not intended to be the sole source of funding for an activity. 
Eligible applicants are also encouraged to seek funding from other sources, including 
fundraising, sponsorships, donations, and/or Federal/Provincial grant programs. 
Applicants who have, or will have, funding from alternate sources must disclose this 
funding as a part of the budget submitted in support of the Community Grant Program 
Application. If no other sources of funding have been pursued, applicants are required 
to provide information on the reasons why other opportunities were not explored. 
Applicants seeking up to a maximum of $500 are not required to submit a budget with 
their application. Any applicant seeking between $500 - $5,000 must provide a budget 
with their application to clearly show how Community Grant funds will be used. 
A successful recipient of the Community Grant program may receive a cash Grant of up 
to $5,000 for the activity. As a guide, Council will normally only provide Grant funds up 
to 25% of the project budget, or $5,000, whichever is the lesser amount. For projects 
where there is a demonstrated significant, unique, or exceptional financial need, and 
where 25% of the project budget is less than $5,000, Council may waive the 25% 
granting cap and approve Grant funds up to $5,000. 
Through the Community Grant Program, Council may approve the provision of "in-kind" 
fee-waivers to a maximum of $2,000 per applicant. For clarification, building and 
planning fees are not eligible to be waived under the Community Grant Program.

8.0 
Application Process 
Information relevant to the Grants process including application due dates and 
guidelines to apply will be advertised in local media and on the Town website at 
www.southbrucepeninsula.com 
The funding call will occur once per year, usually commencing in the month of 
September. Grants awarded will cover the period January - December of the following 
year. 
All organizations must complete the application form in full which means that each 
question must be answered and all the requested supporting documentation must be 
submitted. Incomplete applications may not be considered. The Town reserves the right 
to contact any organization for information which requires clarification. 
Applications must be received by the Town on or before 4:00 pm on the advertised 
submission deadline. No late applications will be considered . It is the sole responsibility 
of the applicant to ensure that the Town receives completed applications. 
Eligible organizations can submit only one (1) application per year. 
Requests for in-kind grants such as waiving of Town fees or use of municipal facilities 
should be accompanied with a dollar value estimate that has been confirmed with the 
applicable Town Department.

9.0 
Evaluation of Applications 
The Town operating budget will be approved with a funding envelope for Community 
Grants. 
The evaluation of applications can take place after budget approval. It is not necessary 
to have the allocations to specific Grant recipients included in the Town budget. 
Eligible applications will be evaluated based on the following criteria: 
• 
How the activity will support the Town's strategic priorities; 
• 
Contribution to the community and impact to residents of the Town by 
strengthening our community and growing our economy; 
• 
Evidence of support from other partners, volunteers and other sources of 
funding to enable the organization or activity to be sustainable; 
• 
Additional financial and non-financial resources being leveraged from other 
sources; 
• 
Evidence that the organization needs the funding. Organizations that have 
budgets or financial statements indicating reserves or a surplus will be 
required to provide explanations of the surplus and how the organization 
intends to use it; 
• 
Sound organizational track record. This considers if the organization has the 
ability, skills and capacity to undertake the activity; 
• 
That the activities do not unnecessarily duplicate successful efforts that 
already exist in the community; 
• 
Sustainability of the organization and activity as applicable; and 
• 
The amount of funding requested by applicants and the funding available in 
the program. 
All applicants will receive notification of Council's decision of whether or not their 
application was successful.

10.0 
Obligations of Grant Recipients 
Applicants awarded a Grant will be held accountable for the expenditure of the funds in 
accordance with the stated objectives/plans. Grants in future years will be reviewed 
based on past demonstrated fiscal responsibility of the applicants. 
Funds granted under this program are not transferable between projects or groups 
without prior Council consent and must be used for the specific purposes outlined in 
Council's original approval. 
In the case of a project's cancellation, repayment of the entire amount of the Community 
Grant will be required. Community Grant funds must be used for the specific purposes 
outlined in the application. Misuse of funds may result in the applicant being disqualified 
from receiving a Grant for a period of not less than two years. 
Successful applicants must provide a report on the program no later than 90 days 
following completion of the program, or by November 30th of the granting year, 
whichever comes first. The final report must certify that funds were spent on activities 
described in the Grant application and must also: 
• 
Include a complete and accurate financial report for the program, outlining the 
detailed project budget compared to the actual income and the actual expenses. 
• 
Clearly indicate those specific expenses that Community Grant funds were uses 
to offset. 
• 
Be signed and authorized by a representative with legal or financial signing 
authority for the organization. 
• 
Include a description of the outcome of the project and an evaluation of the 
success of the project. 
Reports will be forwarded to Town Council for review. 
If all funds are not expended by November 30th of the granting year and will be used in 
December of the granting year, the final report must explain the use of the grants in 
December and the grant recipient should contact staff at the end of the year to provide 
confirmation that all grant funds were expended, as required .

Subject: August Concert Series Bluewater Park 
Recommendation: 
That Council approves $5,000 to be drawn from the Municipal Accommodation Tax 
Reserve, Account 34012 for the purpose of a Thursday night concert series at the Bluewater 
Park Bandshell for the month of August; 
And further that if sponsors are confirmed for the concert series, sponsorship funds will be 
allocated to the Municipal Accommodation Tax Reserve. 
Link to Strategic Planning: Goal 4: Healthy, Vibrant and Safe Communities 
4.1 Enhance facilities for healthy living and affordable and cultural opportunities. 
Background: 
As part of a successful grant application through the Federal Economic Development 
Agency of Southern Ontario's Community Revitalization stream, the Town of South Bruce 
Peninsula was awarded $375,000. These funds are designated for upgrades to Bluewater 
Park, including improvements to the pier and causeway, accessibility enhancements, the 
bandshell, and indigenous and marine interpretive signage. 
The bandshell construction is now complete, and on July 11, 2024, the Town hosted a 
grand opening event at Bluewater Park. Local musicians Midnight Blue performed at the 
concert, and the event was a resounding success, attracting over 400 attendees to the 
ribbon-cutting ceremony and the concert. 
The long-term goal for the bandshell is to encourage rentals for regular concerts and events, 
thereby attracting visitors and creating a positive economic impact on the local economy. 

The rental rate for the bandshell is set at $150 for not-for-profit events and $450 for for-profit 
events. 
In collaboration with a local musician, staff have organized a concert series featuring various 
artists on Thursday evenings from 7:30 pm to 9:00 pm during the month of August, with 
performances scheduled for the 8th, 15th, 22nd, and 29th. This concert series aims to 
showcase the new venue and generate interest in future rentals. 
With the summer season well underway, staff have worked expeditiously to organize this 
series in advance of the first concert date on August 8th. For future Town-run events, staff 
will seek sponsorship to support these initiatives. 
Staff are recommending that the total project budget of $5,000 to fund this concert series be 
drawn from the Municipal Accommodation Tax working capital reserve as these events 
support a tourism attraction in South Bruce Peninsula. 
Staff are also seeking sponsorship for the Thursday night music series and if successful, the 
initiative will be partially/fully funded via sponsorship. At the Time of writing this report, 
sponsorship funding has not been secured, hence the request to utilize MAT funds. Any 
sponsorship funding will be utilized to pay for the concert series and replenish MAT 
reserves, if funding comes at a later date. 
Options: 
A 
$5,000 to be allocated from the Municipal Accommodation Tax Reserve for the 
Thursday night concert series at the Bluewater Park Bandshell in the month of 
August. 
B. Provide alternate direction. 
Attachments: 
None 
Inter-Departmental Impact: 
The Manager of Economic Development will work with the Recreation and Parks 
Department on venue booking and equipment set up. Communications of the concert series 
will be through the website and social media channels. 
Financial Implications:

The funding for this series would be a maximum project budget of $5,000 or $1 ,250 per 
concert. The Town maintains a Municipal Accommodation Tax Reserve, Account 
34012, the funds of which can be utilized as determined by Council. The uncommitted 
balance of the Reserve is $70,935. 

Expected Date of Completion: 
The concert series would be held every Thursday for the month of August, being on the 8th , 
15th , and 22nd with the final concert in the series being on 29th of 2024.

Link to Strategic Planning Goal 1: Transparent and Accountable Governance. 
Background: Status updates on approved capital projects serve as a monitoring 
mechanism for staff and provide information to Council. This represents best practice in 
open and accountable municipal operations. 
Council will be able to track the status of projects that have been approved for completion 
with taxpayer's money and grant money received by the municipality. 
A Capital Status Update was distributed to Directors and operational Managers on July 22nd , 
2024. They were asked to provide a status update and project comments to share with 
Council. This is an opportunity to identify any project challenges and whether the project 
can still be completed on schedule and on budget. 
On November 21St, 2023, Council passed By-Law 78-2023 to adopt the 2024 Operating 
and Capital Budget. 
Analysis: 
The Capital Budget for 2024 identified 46 projects totalling $7,210,500. On December 
19th , 2023 Council received report FS-26-2023 being a report to request the carry-
forward of capital projects to 2024. Based on preliminary figures, 51 capital projects 
totalling $7,571 ,235 were identified and approved for carry-forward. After processing all 
invoices for 2023, the budget carry-forward for these 51 projects was $5,432,045. 

Moving forward with 2024 there are 105 capital projects with an approved budget of 
$14,540,096, compared to 2023 with 100 projects totalling $17,160,341: 
• 
51 projects carried forward from 2023 - $5,432,045 
• 
46 approved projects for 2024 - $7,210,500 
• 
5 in-year approvals by resolution - $1,858,307 
• 
4 operating projects capitalized - $39,244

Subject: Wiarton District Optimist Club Community Grant Program Final Report -
Canada Day Event Support 
Recommendation: That Council receives the final report from the Wiarton District Optimist 
Club as it relates to the Community Grant Program allocation to support the Wiarton Canada 
Day event. 
Link to Strategic Planning: Goal 1: Transparent and Accountable Governance, Goal 
3: Collaboration and Partnerships and Goal 4: Healthy, Vibrant and Safe Communities 
would be the general links to the Strategic Plan. 
Specific Objectives and Actions would be: 
3.1 
Maximize Shared Services and Resources 
3.1.1 Explore formal and informal opportunities to collaborate for expanded service 
delivery, reduced cost and improved community benefit 
Background: The Community Grant Program Policy (TR.18.2) was adopted by Council 
in 2021 as a means to streamline the requests that Council receives from members of 
the community seeking funding . The policy has undergone amendments since its initial 
adoption with the last amendment being adopted in 2024. One of the requirements in 
the policy is that the grant recipients are required to make a final report 90 days 
following their event or by November 30, 2024, whichever is earlier. 
The 2024 program application period closed on November 30, 2023 with eighteen (18) 
submissions being received. Two of the applicants did not receive funding as they did not 
meet the program criteria, proposing projects for Town and other Government Agency 
property. Subsequent to deliberations, Council adopted resolution R-07-2024 wherein 
funding awards were decided and additionally, Council decided to remove the previous 
"automatically recurring" grants which staff had been including in the annual budgets. Using 
the last remaining budget allocation, Council has also provided funding support to two 
additional organizations since the original allocation of funding. 

Staff have received the final report from the Wiarton District Optimist Club which supported 
the annual Canada Day event held in Bluewater Park. The grant allocation was $500. 
The final report from the Wiarton District Optimist Club explains that the event had vendors, 
a BBQ, a pancake breakfast and family entertainment. The Wiarton District Optimist Club 
was fortunate in that they secured several local sponsors and funding through the Celebrate 
Canada Grant Program. All of the funds, including those from the Town allowed them to 
hold a family friendly event which they feel was a success. The Optimist Club was able to 
finish the event with a surplus of $2,839.08. The Town's donation was directed toward the 
Bluewater Park rental costs. 
Options: 
a) 
Receive the final report, as presented. 
b) 
Seek additional information from the Wiarton District Optimist Club.

Inter-departmental Impact: The Legislative Services Department manages the Council 
budget. The Community Grant Program is included as part of the Council budget. The 
Parks, Recreation and Culture Department have many detailed discussions with community 
groups and provides encouragement to those groups to apply for funding . The Legislative 
Services Department collects applications and, together with the Parks, Recreation and 
Culture Department, analyzes them against the policy criteria. The Legislative Services 
Department makes recommendations to Council and provides to Council, the final reports 
from the grant recipients. The Financial Services Department processes the award 
payments.

Community Grant Program. 
The Wiarton District Optimist Club was awarded $500 to support the Canada Day event 
Bluewater Park facility rental. They have demonstrated that the Town funds have been 
expended. 
Expected Date of Completion: Upon resolution of Council unless Council requires 
additional information from the organization. If that is the case, staff will bring an additional 
report to a future meeting.

Community Grant Program 
1.0 
Purpose 
The Town of South Bruce Peninsula has established the Community Grant Program to: 
• 
Improve the well-being of individuals, neighbourhoods and the municipality as 
a whole by directing Community Grant funding to eligible recipients who can 
demonstrate the greatest need in the community while supporting Council's 
strategic priorities. 
• 
Diversify the availability of activities available to all residents of our 
community and contribute to enhancing the quality of life. 
• 
Through this support, it is hoped that other funding may be leveraged, and 
participants and volunteers can be supported, attracted and retained. 
• 
Ensure that the process to review and allocate Community Grant funding is 
transparent, consistent and achieves the optimal impact for the investment 
provided. 
2.0 
Authority 
This policy is established pursuant to Section 107 of the Municipal Act, 2001 which 
allows a municipality, subject to Section 106, to make grants, on such terms as to 
security and otherwise as the Council considers appropriate, to any person, group or 
body, including a fund , within or outside the boundaries of the municipality for any 
purpose that Council considers to be in the interests of the municipality. 
3.0 
Budget 
On an annual basis, Council will determine the total funding envelope for Community 
Grants as part of the annual operating budget. 
As the number of grant requests may exceed funds available and budget priorities may 
change from year to year, applicants are not guaranteed funding . A Community Grant 
approved in any year is not considered a commitment by the Town to continue financial 
assistance in future years.

4.0 
Activities Eligible for Funding 
The Community Grant Program will provide grants to support eligible community-based 
organizations for community-based activities. 
Applications must align with one or more of the Town's strategic priorities. 
An activity funded by a Community Grant must be open to the public at minimal or no 
charge and must be accessible to all community members by satisfying the 
requirements of the Ontario Human Rights Code, the Charter of Rights and Freedoms, 
and the Accessibility for Ontarians with Disabilities Act. 
The Community Grant Program is intended to provide funding that is supplemental to 
the overall financial requirements to carry on a planned activity. The Community Grant 
Program is not intended to be the sole source of funding for an activity. 
Eligible applicants are also encouraged to seek funding from other sources, including 
fundraising, sponsorships, donations, and/or Federal/Provincial grant programs. 
Applicants who have, or will have, funding from alternate sources must disclose this 
funding as a part of the budget submitted in support of the Community Grant Program 
Application. If no other sources of funding have been pursued, applicants are required 
to provide information on the reasons why other opportunities were not explored. 
Applicants seeking up to a maximum of $500 are not required to submit a budget with 
their application. Any applicant seeking between $500 - $5,000 must provide a budget 
with their application to clearly show how Community Grant funds will be used. 
A successful recipient of the Community Grant program may receive a cash Grant of up 
to $5,000 for the activity. As a guide, Council will normally only provide Grant funds up 
to 25% of the project budget, or $5,000, whichever is the lesser amount. For projects 
where there is a demonstrated significant, unique, or exceptional financial need, and 
where 25% of the project budget is less than $5,000, Council may waive the 25% 
granting cap and approve Grant funds up to $5,000. 
Through the Community Grant Program, Council may approve the provision of "in-kind" 
fee-waivers to a maximum of $2,000 per applicant. For clarification, building and 
planning fees are not eligible to be waived under the Community Grant Program.

6.0

Community Grants cannot be used for: 
• 
Accumulated deficits, annual operating losses, debt retirement and/or debt 
servicing costs, financing charges. 
• 
Donations to third-parties and charitable organizations. 
• 
Increasing endowment funds. 
• 
Funding requests of more than $5,000 per organization in any single Grant cycle. 
• 
Retroactive payments - activities or costs incurred before Grants are approved. 
• 
Costs associated with any activity that will be located or held outside of the 
Town.(unless otherwise approved by Council) 
• 
Improvements to property owned, leased or otherwise managed by the Federal 
Government, Provincial Government and any municipal government including the 
Town 
• 
Any project as determined by the Town, that falls under the scope or jurisdiction 
of another municipality, the Federal Government, the Provincial Government 
and/or demonstrates a better alignment with another grant funding organization.

The Town operating budget will be approved with a funding envelope for Community

How the activity will support the Town's strategic priorities; 
• 
Contribution to the community and impact to residents of the Town by 
strengthening our community and growing our economy; 
• 
Evidence of support from other partners, volunteers and other sources of 
funding to enable the organization or activity to be sustainable; 
• 
Additional financial and non-financial resources being leveraged from other 
sources; 
• 
Evidence that the organization needs the funding. Organizations that have 
budgets or financial statements indicating reserves or a surplus will be 
required to provide explanations of the surplus and how the organization 
intends to use it; 
• 
Sound organizational track record. This considers if the organization has the 
ability, skills and capacity to undertake the activity; 
• 
That the activities do not unnecessarily duplicate successful efforts that 
already exist in the community; 
• 
Sustainability of the organization and activity as applicable; and 
• 
The amount of funding requested by applicants and the funding available in 
the program.

application was successful.

Obligations of Grant Recipients 
Applicants awarded a Grant will be held accountable for the expenditure of the funds in 
accordance with the stated objectives/plans. Grants in future years will be reviewed 
based on past demonstrated fiscal responsibility of the applicants. 
Funds granted under this program are not transferable between projects or groups 
without prior Council consent and must be used for the specific purposes outlined in

Grant will be required. Community Grant funds must be used for the specific purposes

from receiving a Grant for a period of not less than two years. 
Successful applicants must provide a report on the program no later than 90 days 
following completion of the program, or by November 30th of the granting year, 
whichever comes first. The final report must certify that funds were spent on activities 
described in the Grant application and must also: 
• 
Include a complete and accurate financial report for the program, outlining the 
detailed project budget compared to the actual income and the actual expenses. 
• 
Clearly indicate those specific expenses that Community Grant funds were uses 
to offset. 
• 
Be signed and authorized by a representative with legal or financial signing 
authority for the organization. 
• 
Include a description of the outcome of the project and an evaluation of the 
success of the project. 
Reports will be forwarded to Town Council for review. 
If all funds are not expended by November 30th of the granting year and will be used in 
December of the granting year, the final report must explain the use of the grants in 
December and the grant recipient should contact staff at the end of the year to provide 
confirmation that all grant funds were expended, as required .

Council Meetings
Regular Council Meetings typically occur on the 2nd and 4th Wednesday of each month, with exceptions made during holidays. In the months of July, August, and December, Regular Council Meetings are held only once per month. Regular Council Meetings are open to the public and live streamed to YouTube.

Committee of Council Meetings
Committees of Council meet as directed in each committees terms of reference. Meetings and agendas can be found using the calendar below. Additionally, visit the Committees of Council webpage for information such as mandates, members, minutes and more! 
Types of Meetings
Meetings Open to the Public: Almost all regular Council and Committee meetings are Open to the Public.  The public is welcome to attend and observe.  These meetings follow a set agenda with all information being presented or discussed published in advance. There isn't a formal opportunity for observers to speak to Council or Committee members during these meetings.  If you have thoughts or concerns about a topic on the agenda, let staff, Council or Committee members know them before the meeting takes place. 
 Public Meetings: A Public Meeting is a special meeting where members of the public can attend and speak directly to Council or a Committee as part of the agenda. Comments from the public are formally documented as part of the meeting record. In some cases (like zoning changes), a public meeting is legally required under the Planning Act.  Council can also hold a Public Meeting when they want direct input on other issues.Come prepared to share your thoughts when you attend a Public Meeting!  
 Open House: An Open House is informal by design. The public is welcome to attend, ask questions and share feedback. There is no agenda or formal record.  An Open House is the chance to have a one-on-one conversation with the people working on the issue.

Township of South Frontenac By-Law 2023-04 
 
A By-Law To Define The Mandate And Meeting Procedures For Committees  
Established By The Township of South Frontenac 
 
Passed:  January 31, 2023 
Whereas By-law 2025-21, ‘Procedural By-law’ establishes the rules and procedures under 
which Council and Committees of Council are to operate; and, 
Whereas Council has established committees and boards that are comprised of both 
members of the public and members of Council; 
Now Therefore Be It Resolved That the Council of The Corporation of the Township of 
South Frontenac enacts as follows: 
1.0 Application of the Committee By-law 
 
1.1 Code of Conduct 
 
 
All members of Council and members of the public appointed by the Township of South 
Frontenac to a board, committee or community committee outlined in the Committee By-
law must abide to By-law 2019-12, A By-Law to Adopt A Council Code Of Conduct, 
Complaint Protocol And A Council Staff Relationship Policy And Delegate To The 
Integrity Commissioner The Authority To Impose Penalties Under The Code Of Conduct. 
1.2 Use of Terms; “Agency”, “Board” and “Committee”  
The use of the terms “Agency”, “Committee” and “Board” shall be used interchangeably 
for the purpose of the Committee By-law. 
2.0 Policy For Creating, Amending or Dissolving a Committee, Sub-Committee or 
Working Group 
2.1 Procedure 
Council may create a new committee, amend an existing committee and/or its mandate/terms 
of reference, or dissolve an existing committee in accordance with the following sub-sections. 
A non-statutory advisory committee shall not extend beyond the term of Council unless the 
newly elected Council confirms by resolution the continuance of the committee. 
 
 

Township of South Frontenac By-Law Number 2023-04 “Committee By-law”         Page 4 of 25 
2.2 Creating a Committee - Council may create a new committee in response to any of the 
following: 
(a) 
Requirements of applicable legislation or regulation (Federal, Provincial or Municipal By-
law); 
(b) 
Changing priorities; 
(c) 
To address significant public issues or trends; 
(d) 
Where public input is deemed desirable; 
(e) 
Recommendation and report by staff; and, 
(f) 
Any other reason deemed appropriate by Council. 
In creating a new committee, Council shall have regard for the following: 
(a) 
Establishing a clearly defined mandate and terms of reference; 
(b) 
Membership and quorum requirements/qualifications; 
(c) 
Composition of the committee; 
(d) 
Alignment with the Strategic Plan, Departmental goals and objectives; 
(e) 
The reporting relationship and frequency of meetings; 
(f) 
Public and financial considerations; 
(g) 
Staff resources to be made available and the impacts on Township Departments; 
(h) 
The need for any sub-committees/working groups; and, 
(i) 
Defined timeline for completion of the assigned tasks (i.e. sunset date). 
2.3 
Amending A Committee and/or Its Mandate 
Amendments to the mandate/terms of reference of a committee may be initiated by Council, 
by resolution of the committee or by a report and recommendation from staff. The following 
factors may be considered by Council when amending a committee’s mandate/terms of 
reference: 
(a) 
Impact of the change on the mandate/terms of reference; 
(b) 
Continued relevance of the committee’s purpose and/or function; 
(c) 
The degree of public interest; 
(d) 
Changes to the applicable legislation or regulations; 
(e) 
Changing Council priorities or new issues at Council; 
(f) 
Cost analysis and required resources; and, 
(g) 
Committee sunset date. 
 
 

Township of South Frontenac By-Law Number 2023-04 “Committee By-law”         Page 5 of 25 
2.4 
Dissolving A Committee 
 
The dissolving of a committee may be triggered by any one of the following: 
(a) 
Expiration of the committee term; 
(b) 
Completion of the committee’s task or mandate; 
(c) 
Effectiveness of the committee’s operations (e.g. frequency of meetings,  
amount of committee business, number of cancelled meetings); 
(d) 
Resolution of the issues that led to the creation of the Committee; 
(e) 
The legislative requirement for the committee no longer exists; 
(f) 
Merger with another committee; 
(g) 
Changing Council priorities; 
(h) 
Recommendation by the committee by resolution; and, 
(i) 
Report and recommendation by staff. 
 
All committees created by Council will be formally dissolved by a Council resolution that is 
implemented through amendments to this By-law as necessary. 
2.5  Establishment of Sub-Committees/Working Groups 
 If it is the desire of the majority of a Committee to establish a Sub-Committee/Working 
Group, a recommendation must be made to Council, either directly or through the 
appropriate Committee for approval of the creation of the Sub-Committee/Working 
Group.   
 
 Included with the recommendation for the establishment of the  
 Sub-Committee/Working Group must be information with respect to: 
 
(a) 
The Sub-Committee/Working Group mandate/terms of reference; 
(b) 
The number of members; 
(c)  
The composition of membership, including members of the public and staff, if 
applicable, and how members are to be recruited; 
(d)  
The reporting structure; 
(e)  
The staff and other resources to be made available; and, 
(f)  
A start and finish date. 
 
A Sub-Committee/Working Group may also be appointed directly by Council.  
Sub-Committee/Working Group authorizations must be reviewed annually by Council.

3.0  Criteria to Serve on Committee 
Citizen appointees to committees listed in this By-law must be at least 18 years or older, 
a resident/business owner in the Township, and be one of the following:  
•  
Canadian Citizen, or  
•  
Permanent Resident, a person who has been given permanent resident status by 
immigrating to Canada but is not a Canadian Citizen, and has resided in the 
Township of South Frontenac for at least one year.  
Appointees must maintain residence in the Township of South Frontenac for the duration 
of their term.  
All appointments made to agencies, boards and commissions listed in Schedule B, C and 
D must be made in accordance with the rules established by their governing body. 
 
3.1 Term of Appointment 
(a) 
Committee members will continue to serve on a committee past the expiration of 
their term until they are replaced.  All Council membership on all Committees end 
on November 14 of a municipal election year. 
(b)   
Terms of office and membership on some external boards / commissions / 
authorities or quasi-judicial committees must be in accordance with this By-Law 
unless the term of office is established under statute, legislation or relevant 
governing body. 
(c) 
The term of appointment is defined by the Committee By-law and confirmed by a 
resolution of Council.  
(d) 
Renewed membership on a committee is not automatic, any member of the 
public who wishes to serve for an additional term must submit the approved 
application form or provide a letter which includes the necessary information in 
order to be considered for re-appointment. 
3.2   Retention of Applications to Serve on Committees 
Applications from members of the public who are not appointed during the regular 
appointment process will be kept on file in the Clerk’s Department for a period of one year

applicants who applied to serve on that Committee and were not appointed will be 
contacted and asked if they are still interested in serving.  Names of those who continue 
to have an interest to serve on the Committee will be submitted to Council for 
consideration to fill the vacancy.  The Clerk’s Department will readvertise the vacancy if 
necessary.

4.0  General Provisions Governing Committees Outlined in Schedule A and 
 
Schedule C

and Schedule C of this By-law must conform to the rules governing the procedures of a

majority affirmative vote of the members of a Committee who are present and voting.

of a Committee (excluding the Committee of the Whole) who are present and voting.

The Clerk or Deputy Clerk shall provide administrative and legislative support to the 
Committee as well as conduct their duties in accordance of the Municipal Act and all 
other relevant legislation.

Clerk or Deputy Clerk.

cause acceptable to the Committee, the absences will be brought to the attention 
of the Clerk.

The Clerk will contact the absent committee member to discuss the reasons for 
absenteeism and to determine whether the member wishes to provide a letter of

Upon confirmation that the member will no longer be serving on the Committee,

  WHEREAS the Garden City Skyway has for generations served as one of the most recognizable gateways to St. Catharines and the Niagara Region, carrying the Queen Elizabeth Way across the Welland Canal between St. Catharines and Niagara-on-the-Lake; and
  WHEREAS the Province of Ontario is undertaking the Garden City Skyway Bridge Twinning Project, which will see a new bridge constructed alongside the existing Skyway and the existing structure subsequently repaired and upgraded; and
  WHEREAS the late Jim Bradley devoted more than five decades of his life to public service, beginning as a member of St. Catharines City Council in 1970, representing St. Catharines in the Legislative Assembly of Ontario from 1977 to 2018, and subsequently serving as a Niagara Regional Councillor and Regional Chair; and
  WHEREAS during his 41 years representing St. Catharines at Queen’s Park, Jim Bradley served in numerous senior positions in the Government of Ontario, including as Minister of Transportation, Minister of the Environment, Minister of Municipal Affairs and Housing, and Minister of Community Safety and Correctional Services; and
  WHEREAS throughout his career, Jim Bradley remained closely identified with St. Catharines and Niagara and dedicated his public life to representing the residents of this community;
  THEREFORE BE IT RESOLVED that St. Catharines City Council respectfully request that the Province of Ontario formally name the completed Garden City Skyway crossing the “James J. Bradley Garden City Skyway,” preserving the historic Garden City Skyway name while permanently recognizing Jim Bradley’s extraordinary record of service to St. Catharines, Niagara and the Province of Ontario; and
  BE IT FURTHER RESOLVED that this resolution be forwarded to the Premier of Ontario, the Minister of Transportation, the local Members of Provincial Parliament, the Regional Municipality of Niagara, and the Town of Niagara-on-the-Lake, requesting their consideration and support.

Speaking at a Council Meeting
SECTION MENU
Council welcomes and encourages members of the public to speak on matters of interest to them at meetings. Individuals can address Council as a Delegation, during Open Forum or at a Public Meeting. 
Speaking as a Delegation
Individuals who want to speak at a Council meeting, can submit a delegation request using our online form. Request are required to be submitted by noon the Wednesday prior to the Council meeting one wishes to speak at.
Delegation will have 15 minutes to address Council. Prior to registering as a delegation, you may want to discuss your concerns with our staff as issues may be outside the Township’s jurisdiction and more appropriately brought before another level of government or public agency.
Speaking During Open Forum 
During Open Forum, any person may address Council on any matter that is listed on the agenda except items that will be subject to a statutory public meeting pursuant to the Planning Act on the same agenda.
Open Forum participants will have three (3) minutes to address Council.
Speaking During a Statutory Public Meeting
Any person who attends a public meeting may address Council on any item listed under Statutory Public Meeting without the provision of notice. Members of the public who wish to make oral submissions with respect to an application that is the subject of the statutory public meeting shall be limited to speaking not more than five minutes per person, per application.

Terms of Reference 
 
Definitions 
For the purposes of these Terms of Reference, the following definitions shall apply:  
a)  “Township” means the Municipal Corporation of the Township of Tay;   
b) “Committee” means the Agricultural Advisory Committee;   
c)  “Council” means the governing body of the Township;   
d) “Councillor” means an elected official of the Township, including the Mayor;  
e)  “Mayor” means the chief elected official of the Township;   
f)  “Member” means an individual appointed to the Committee;   
g) “Municipal Act” means the Municipal Act, 2001, as amended;   
h) “Procedural By-law” means the Township By-law which provides the Rules of  
Procedure for Council and its Committees.   
    
Purpose   
As a Committee of Council, the role of the Agricultural Advisory Committee is to provide 
agricultural perspectives related to municipal operations and practices. 
Responsibilities  
The mandate and responsibilities of the Committee are as follows:  
a) Provide input related to the agricultural community; 
b) Provide input on the implementation of Provincial and Federal legislation, policies 
and guidelines related to the agricultural industry; 
c) Provide input on agricultural and rural policy directions pursued by the Township of 
Tay. This may include providing advice on municipally initiated official plan 
amendments related to agricultural matters, on local agricultural matters through 
an official plan review, or other policy directions pursued by the Township; 
d) Provide input on the identification and implementation of programs which 
encourage public awareness and education of agricultural and related rural issues; 
and, 
e) Provide input on matters as they arise at the request of Council.

Composition  
The Committee shall consist of a minimum of five (5) voting members, being a minimum of 
three (3) citizen members from the agriculture community, one (1) Council representative, 
and one (1) member who represents the Simcoe County Federation of Agriculture.  
Citizen member appointments shall be adopted by Council at the first Regular Council 
Meeting of each term.   
 
In accordance with the Township’s Procedural By-law, the Mayor shall be an ex-officio 
Member of each Committee and have the same rights as the other Committee Members, 
including the right to vote.   
Staff representation shall consist of the Municipal Clerk and/or their designate and other 
staff resources, as required. Staff shall be non-voting members and shall not be included 
to establish quorum. Staff responsibilities as they relate to this committee are limited to 
agenda creation and minutes recording, as well as related internal administrative 
processes.   
Committee members shall be appointed by By-law for the term of Council, four (4) years, 
and until their successors are appointed. In the event that a membership vacancy 
presents itself during the Term of the Committee, Council shall fill the vacancy by 
appointment without the need to advertise.   
Chair/Vice-Chair  
At its first meeting of each term of office, the Committee shall elect a Chair and Vice-Chair 
from among its citizen members. If the role of the Chair becomes vacant for any reason 
during a term of office, the Committee shall elect a new Chairperson from among its   
citizen members.   
The Vice-Chair shall assume the role of the Chair in their absence.  
Quorum  
A majority of voting members are required to be present to constitute a quorum.  
Meetings  
The Committee shall adopt the meeting schedule for the year at the first meeting of each 
year, if not adopted in the final meeting of the previous year.   
The Committee will formally meet two (2) times per year; once in March and once in 
November. Additional meetings shall be scheduled as considered necessary by the 
Committee or Chair.

by the Committee, the Chair shall contact the Member in writing to confirm whether they 
wish to continue serving on the Committee and commit to the remainder of their term.

recommendations for amendments prior to the appointment of the new Committee.

 f)  “Internal Controls” means systems, processes, and procedures developed to:

Purpose   
As a Committee of Council, the Audit Committee will be responsible for overseeing all 
material aspects of the Township’s financial reporting, control, and audit functions.   
The Committee will focus on the qualitative aspects of financial reporting and on the 
Township’s processes for the management of financial risk and for compliance with 
significant applicable legal, ethical, and regulatory requirements. The Committee provides 
a focal point for communication between Council, the independent auditor, and 
management, and facilitates an impartial, objective, and independent review of 
management practices.   
Responsibilities  
The Committee shall:  
a)  Review and assess the annual financial statements before they are brought forward  
to Council;

management to address such matters, related auditors’ views, and the basis for

c)  Recommend changes to important accounting principles and the application thereof  
in annual financial reports;   
d) Review reports from the independent auditors as well as any audit problems or   
difficulties and management’s response;   
e)  Maintain strong, positive working relationships with management, independent auditors  
and other advisors.   
The Committee may request a report from the Treasurer on matters within its mandate 
and within approved budgets.   
When the Committee reviews a report it may:  
a)  Receive it for information;   
b) Send it to Council with or without recommendations;   
c)  Request additional information about matters relating to the report before sending  
it to Council with or without recommendations.

Review and assess the Township’s business and financial risk management process, 
including the adequacy of the overall control environment and controls in selected areas 
representing significant risk.   
Review and assess the Township’s system of internal controls for detecting accounting and 
financial reporting errors, fraud and defalcations, legal violations, and non-compliance with 
the corporate code of conduct.   
Review the related findings and recommendations of the independent auditors, together 
with management’s responses.

are reported to the committee.

affect their objectivity or independence.

Terms of Reference   
 
Definitions 
For the purposes of these Terms of Reference, the following definitions shall apply:  
a)  “Township” means the Municipal Corporation of the Township of Tay;   
b) “Committee” means the Committee of Adjustment;   
c)  “Council” means the governing body of the Township;

f)  “Member” means an individual appointed to the Committee;

h) “Procedural By-law” means the Township By-law which provides the Rules of  
Procedure for Council and its’ Committees.   
    
Purpose   
The Committee of Adjustment is a statutory tribunal with authority delegated to it by 
Township of Tay Council, under the provisions of the Ontario Planning Act, to hold public 
hearings to make decisions on applications submitted to the Township’s Planning and 
Development Services Department for minor variances, alterations in legal non-
conforming uses and consents or severances. The Committee operates independently 
from Council and its decisions may be appealed to the Ontario Land Tribunal. Committee 
of Adjustment Members will also sit as a Property Standards Committee to deal with the 
Property Standards By-law and will also sit as Fence-viewers to deal with fence matters 
under the Line Fences Act.   
Committee Mandate  
The Committee of Adjustment is a quasi-judicial body, somewhat court-like in its   
operation, charged with observance and protection of applicable planning law and also   
with protecting the rights of the individuals affected by the decisions made. The common 
law principles of natural justice require the Committee of Adjustment to ensure that 
individuals affected by their decisions have their equivalent of “a day in court”. The 
Committee must also satisfy legal requirements concerning notice, public hearings, calling 
of witnesses, notices of decisions and recording of proceedings. As well as the legal 
procedures detailed in the Planning Act, the Municipal Act, the Statutory Powers Procedure 
Act, the Municipal Conflict of Interest Act and the Municipal Freedom of Information and 
Protection of Privacy Act govern the Committee of Adjustment.

the Township of Tay Council through the Township’s Official Plan, the Township’s Zoning 
By-law, the County of Simcoe’s Official Plan and Policies approved by the Province of 
Ontario. 
The goal of the Committee of Adjustment is to provide for and conduct a fair hearing by: 
  
 
 
• 
Allowing anyone wishing to speak to an application an opportunity to do so; 
• 
Giving due diligence to the consideration of each application;   
• 
Openly having all discussions about each application and making all decisions in public   
• 
at the hearing;   
• 
Making rational decisions with appropriate, well-thought-out conditions; and   
• 
Clearly stating the reasons for their decisions.

North Shore Compliance Audit Committee 
The Compliance Audit Committee is an independent statutory body that reviews and decides on 
applications for audits of municipal election campaign finances. The municipalities of Terrace Bay, 
Marathon, Manitouwadge and Schreiber are currently seeking qualified individuals to serve as members 
on the North Shore Compliance Audit Committee (NSCAC) for the 2026 Municipal Election. 
 
Who should apply: 
Applications are encouraged from individuals with experience in: 
• 
Law and investigations 
• 
Accounting or auditing 
• 
Finance 
• 
Compliance, governance 
• 
Public administration 
• 
Municipal government 
 
Under the Municipal Elections Act, 1996, municipal employees and officers, members of council or 
local boards, election candidates, and registered third parties are not eligible to serve on the North 
Shore Compliance Audit Committee. 
 
What Does a Compliance Audit Committee Do?  
The Compliance Audit Committee reviews and makes decisions regarding applications for 
compliance audits of campaign finances for Council candidates and registered third party advertisers 
in municipal elections and by-elections.  The committee can: 
• 
Determine whether an elector’s application for a compliance audit should be granted or rejected 
• 
Appoint a qualified auditor if an application is approved 
• 
Receive and reviewing the auditor’s report 
• 
Decide whether legal proceedings should be initiated where a contravention appears to have 
occurred 
• 
Determine whether audit costs should be recovered from the applicant if no contravention is found 
and the application lacked reasonable grounds 
 
The Committee also reviews reports from the Clerk identifying contributors who may have exceeded 
contribution limits and determines whether legal action should be considered.

from each of the participating communities, depending on qualifications

Project Information 
 
1. Purpose 
 
The Corporation of the Township of Terrace Bay is seeking quotations for the supply and installation of 
a new security camera system to replace its existing dated system. 
The Township is seeking a reliable, modern and expandable security camera system that includes all 
equipment, software, installation and support required for operation, together with as many priority 
cameras as can reasonably be provided within the available project budget. The system must also 
allow additional cameras or locations to be added in the future. 
 
2. Project Objectives 
 
The Township’s objectives for this project are to: 
 
• 
Replace the Township’s dated camera system with a modern digital system;  
• 
Provide a complete and operational system, including all required equipment, software, licensing, 
installation and support;  
• 
Replace as many of the Township’s priority existing cameras as reasonably possible within the 
available project budget;  
• 
Provide secure and user-friendly access to live and recorded footage;  
• 
Identify any internet, networking and ongoing service requirements associated with the proposed 
system; and  
• 
Establish a system that can accommodate additional cameras and municipal locations in the future. 
 
3. Project Locations and Priorities 
 
The current project includes existing cameras at the following municipal locations: 
• 
Terrace Bay Community Centre;  
• 
Terrace Bay Swimming Pool; and  
• 
Simcoe Plaza, where two existing cameras are located.  
Priority will be given to replacing the existing cameras at these locations, together with the equipment, 
software and infrastructure required to provide a complete and operational system. 
One existing outdoor camera operates separately from the system being replaced and can already be 
accessed remotely. Replacement or integration of this camera is considered a lower priority and may 
be proposed if the available project budget permits. 
The final number of cameras replaced will be determined based on the proposed system requirements, 
site conditions and available project budget. Proponents may recommend alternative camera 
placements where they would provide more effective coverage. 
Future expansion to the Cultural Centre, Tourist Information Centre, Lighthouse or other municipal 
locations is addressed in Section 5. 
 
4. Scope of Work 
 
The successful proponent will complete the following work: 

• 
Review the existing camera locations, equipment and site conditions at the Terrace Bay Community 
Centre, Terrace Bay Swimming Pool and Simcoe Plaza;  
• 
Recommend an appropriate system design and camera placement;  
• 
Supply and install a complete digital security camera system, including cameras, recording and 
storage equipment, software, licensing, cabling, mounts, power supplies and all other required 
components;  
• 
Replace or remove existing equipment where required for the new installation;  
• 
Identify any internet connection, networking, subscription, licensing or other ongoing service 
requirements and associated costs;  
• 
Configure and test the completed system;  
• 
Provide authorized Township staff with secure access to live and recorded footage;  
• 
Provide system documentation, warranty information and staff training;  
• 
Include as many priority camera replacements as reasonably possible within the available budget 
while ensuring the base quotation provides a complete and operational system; and  
• 
Provide a prioritized expansion plan with separately itemized pricing for any priority camera 
replacements that cannot be included in the base quotation.  
The proposed system must be capable of accommodating additional cameras and municipal locations 
without requiring premature replacement of the central recording, storage or management equipment. 
5. Optional and Future Services 
Proponents may provide separate pricing or planning information for the following: 
• 
Replacement or integration of the newer independently operated outdoor camera;  
• 
Future security camera coverage at the Terrace Bay Cultural Centre, Tourist Information Centre, 
Terrace Bay Lighthouse or other municipal locations;  
• 
Public-facing HD livestream coverage at Terrace Bay Beach or the Terrace Bay Lighthouse;  
• 
Livestream capability at the arena for tournaments and events; and  
• 
Livestream capability at the curling club for bonspiels and events.  
These items must be identified and priced separately and must not reduce the equipment, installation 
or priority camera replacements included in the base quotation. This information is requested for future 
planning purposes and may not form part of the work awarded under this RFQ.

The Township of Tiny is pleased to offer live streaming of council meetings. Live streaming and the subsequent video file are provided as a convenience to our community. Please note, as per the Live streaming Protocol, meetings of Boards and Advisory Committees of Council will not be live streamed or audio recorded with the exception of the Committee of Adjustment meetings. Due to its quasi-judicial nature, the Committee of Adjustment meetings will be live streamed only and not archived.
Technical difficulties will be experienced at times.  We will do our best to address them immediately, but video, audio, and recording systems may malfunction.
